keep.why: Adds a caveat: even in a recharge oscillator model, timing of strong El Niños can be unpredictable despite heat accumulation.
This paper finds a mechanism that can make strong El Niño events unpredictable, supporting the dashboard's caveat that past events are no guide here.
This early warning study forecasts a moderate-to-strong El Niño for 2023 with an 89 percent onset chance, adding an independent forecast to the event assessment.
Explains how a temperature difference across the equatorial Pacific can distinguish the eastern Pacific type of El Niño from the central Pacific type.
Shows how the 2017 El Niño's heavy rains and floods disrupted spending in Peru, illustrating economic harm on South America's coast.
Cautions that the strength of extreme events like those in 1982 and 1997 can switch unpredictably, limiting forecasts of harsh impacts.
Forecast before 2023 that El Niño would add about 0.2°C and likely make 2024 the hottest year on record.
Shows 2023's global warmth was also driven by record-low albedo, a caveat to attributing all warming to El Niño.
It shows how the ocean and atmosphere exchange energy, which creates El Niño's global weather signature.
It links large scale air temperature patterns to El Niño phases, showing how atmospheric coupling shapes the event.
It measures how the 2017 El Niño changed consumer spending in Peru, showing economic impacts far from the warm water.
Explains that El Nino raises global temperature by about +0.2C and likely made 2024 the hottest year.
Adds caveat that 2023's warming surge was also driven by record-low sunlight reflection, not just El Nino.
Finds sea surface temperatures rose in sharp persistent steps in 1925/26 and 1987/88 rather than smooth or temporary spikes.
Measures tropical Atlantic sea surface temperature indices and finds strong persistence, supporting a stayed shift rather than a spike.
Explains that record-low planetary albedo from fewer low clouds amplified the recent global temperature surge beyond known drivers.
Uses global temperature data to show an El Nino spike can top the record without starting a new lasting level.
Finds tropical Atlantic sea surface temperature indices are strongly persistent, so rises tend to stay rather than reverse.
Shows in a conceptual model that climate components can cross thresholds and settle into new stable states.
It shows models missed a record low cloud cover that amplified the 2023 heat, so forecasts can lag reality and need upward revisions.
It reports an early warning method that predicted the 2023 El Nino onset and strength, so model forecast shifts can be meaningful.
It explains that scarce observations and climate model biases limit El Niño forecasts, and a hybrid model improves skill.
It shows standard El Niño forecasts lose skill after six months and that machine learning can improve that skill.
It shows that scarce data makes learning El Niño variability hard, but pre-training on climate models helps.
Explains how a warmer upper ocean and stronger layering can strengthen El Nino, so a record hot ocean may mean forecasts see a different system.
It cautions that record-low planetary albedo amplified the 2023 global temperature surge, so other factors can shift the peak warmth.
Bank card data from Peru show El Nino shifted consumer spending and marked a recovery time, matching delayed economic impacts.
Explains that El Nino adds about 0.2 degrees Celsius to global air temperature, so the hottest year comes after onset.
Caveat: low cloud cover also helped cause the 2023 heat spike, so ocean heat is not the only driver.
Finds 2023 warming beat model estimates by 0.2 K and links the gap to record low planetary albedo.
Shows global radiative feedback weakened recently, making observed warming stronger than many models assume.
Shows CFSv2 made a correct monsoon forecast for the wrong physical reason, so a model can score well yet still be biased.
Reports a network model outperforming CFSv2 and SEAS5, supporting that existing seasonal forecast systems can underperform.
It gives a separate 2026 ENSO forecast that also expected neutral or a weak event, illustrating forecasts undershot the observed ONI.
Model biases in the West African monsoon and its ENSO teleconnection help explain the weak mixed rainfall signal.
Shows early winter El Nino can nudge the North Atlantic Oscillation positive and late winter negative, while models struggle with this link.
Shows that El Niño weakens Sahel summer rainfall mainly by cutting heavy daily rain events, the main source of year-to-year variability.
Finds in Sahel croplands that El Niño tends to reduce harvest-time political violence while La Niña increases it, adding nuance to conflict risk.
Maps Iran's seasonal precipitation response to ENSO, PDO and NAO, showing winter is most affected.
Assesses El Niño effects on warm and cold winters in northern Eurasia, supporting the mild European Russia tendency and its limits.
Measures how Eastern Pacific El Niño raises the odds of very dry western and wet central Pacific seasons.
Explains that El Niño type (east or central Pacific warming) switches which Pacific islands get dry or wet.
Links Paraná streamflow variability to solar cycles and El Niño, which can help explain flood risk in the basin.
Develops a method to estimate the baseline averages used for Niño 3.4 temperature anomalies, relevant under climate change.
Forecasts El Niño onset and magnitude from temperature anomaly patterns inside Niño 3.4, showing its predictive value.
Shows eastern Pacific El Niño events bring very high or low seasonal rain over wider areas than central Pacific events, matching stronger coastal impacts.
Uses card transaction data from the 2017 El Niño in Peru to measure how floods changed spending and which merchants were affected.
Measures where El Niño and La Niña make regions warmer or cooler, supporting mirrored weather effects.
Finds La Niña phases raise weather-related power outages in the US, showing its weather impacts.
Shows strong El Nino events can be unpredictably strong, though they peak in northern winter and affect global weather.
Explains how links between air temperature patterns make El Nino grow and then decay after northern winter, so events last about a year.
Measures how El Nino breaks many links in a global climate network, supporting the claim that it changes weather on half the planet.
Explains that zonal sea surface temperature differences in the tropical Pacific can indicate whether an El Niño is central or eastern Pacific type.
It shows standard 30-year normals for Niño 3.4 can be biased under warming, so ONI anomalies may need adjusted baselines.
Shows eastern Pacific events produce broader precipitation anomalies than central Pacific events, so their impacts differ.
Shows eastern and central Pacific El Niño types can be separated early and that their regional rainfall impacts differ.
Explains climate normals as multi-decade averages and anomalies as departures from them, the same concept used for 1991-2020.
Proposes a real-time filter for climate normals and anomalies that accounts for warming trends, improving above-trend anomaly estimates.
Shows the long SOI record contains enough signal to predict ENSO years ahead, supporting its use as an atmospheric ENSO index.
Demonstrates a nonanticipative analog method for forecasting temperature extremes from past observations, no climate model.
Deep learning for extreme events often lacks enough historical data, so it adds physics and simulated data to cope.
A hybrid ML-physics model reproduces ENSO teleconnections but shows deficiencies in nonlinear response and under out-of-distribution warming.
Shows ENSO forecast skill normally falls beyond six months, the basis for treating lead 6 errors as expected.
Measures ENSO phase skill out to 22-24 months, showing lead 6 is not a hard limit for all models.
Shows subsurface heat leads surface warming, supporting the fuel gauge idea.
Explains how climate normals and anomalies are estimated, and warns standard baselines can be biased in a changing climate.
Shows seasonal forecast models capture the ENSO to Atlantic hurricane link but overstate it, meaning it is statistical not deterministic.
Finds El Nino phases produce episodic breakdowns and strong teleconnections, supporting the usual not guaranteed framing.
Links recurring mid latitude circulation patterns to teleconnections, showing the atmospheric rearrangement behind remote links.
Shows climate change has shifted teleconnection patterns, so these statistical links are not fixed.
Shows how equatorial wind stress shifts the ocean's warm layer, supporting the idea that trades are an engine of ENSO.
Explains how seasonal baselines for Niño 3.4 are estimated and warns that standard 30-year normals can be biased under climate change.
It finds a running total of El Nino and La Nina explains about half of tropospheric temperature variation, matching delayed ocean heating.
Shows El Nino shocks during the crop growing season change harvest related conflict only in exposed croplands, so impacts are local and seasonal.
Maps how different El Nino types bring very low or high seasonal rainfall to particular regions, shaping agricultural production there.
Finds El Nino temperature links are concentrated in limited areas and much of the globe is unaffected, so impacts are localized.
Models the ocean atmosphere coupling that gives ENSO its global climate signature and distant impacts.
Questions the standard SOI pressure index and suggests sea surface temperature differences capture atmospheric response better.
Shows a machine learning model reproduces coupled ocean atmosphere dynamics including El Nino, supporting the link.
Explains that standard deterministic SST reconstructions like ERSST may understate observation uncertainty; offers a probabilistic alternative.
In model projections, subsurface warming is linked to later surface warming, supporting the idea that El Nino heat builds below first.
Radiosonde profiles over Italy show temperature oscillations change phase with height and vary by layer, backing the whole air column view.
Models westerly wind bursts as noise that amplifies El Niño, with stronger events having more bursts.
Proposes a real time filter for wind anomalies, useful background for the two sigma threshold.
Finds record low planetary albedo from fewer low clouds boosted absorbed sunlight, helping explain the recent jump in Earth's energy imbalance.
Shows how El Nino wind patterns can create the sea surface temperature pattern of an Indian Ocean Dipole.
Quantifies how El Nino controls the Indian Ocean Dipole, mainly at its peak.
Finds the Indian Ocean Dipole influence on Indian rainfall becomes clearer once El Nino is removed.
Models how MJO wind forcing can trigger ENSO events, supporting the idea that the MJO times the pushes.
Uses a stochastic model to capture interactions between wind, MJO and ENSO, adding evidence for the coupling.
Quantifies how MEI links multiple tropical Pacific variables and tracks coupled variability.
Measures how ENSO crop-growing-season shocks change postharvest conflict in exposed croplands, strongest in Southern Africa and the Sahel.
Shows EP and CP El Niños leave different footprints in extreme seasonal rainfall, with EP affecting larger areas.
Finds the east-west Pacific temperature contrast signals whether an upcoming El Niño will be Eastern or Central Pacific.
Shows how Central and Eastern Pacific El Niño patterns can arise from combined intraseasonal, interannual and decadal processes.
Uses a simple El Niño model to show weak forcing can cause irregular switching that limits strong event predictability.
Finds an intrinsic predictability limit for strong El Niño events from irregular switching between oscillatory and chaotic states.
Shows model skill is limited by missing ENSO nonlinearity, and a nonlinear model from observations improves prediction and reduces the spring predictability barrier.
Notes climate model biases and linear models missing warm-cold asymmetry, and a hybrid model capturing that asymmetry improves ENSO forecasts.
Shows strong El Niño events can be intrinsically unpredictable, so a measured very strong event is an important risk signal.
Shows a model of equatorial Pacific heat buildup and release can make strong El Nino timing unpredictable, a caveat for this gauge.
Shows El Niño has two types with different impacts and that the type can be forecast from a temperature difference across the Pacific.
Found heavy rain and floods during the 2017 El Niño changed consumer spending in Peru, showing economic disruption.
Explains that strong El Niño strength and timing are inherently unpredictable, supporting the statement's caveat that past events are no guide here.
Explains a recent global temperature surge by fewer low clouds, allowing more sunlight to heat the surface and ocean.
Shows El Niño warming peaks the following year, forecasting 2024 as hottest after the 2023 onset.
Adds caveat that record-low cloud cover helped drive the 2023 temperature surge beyond El Niño alone.
Explains that El Niño is a coupling between ocean and atmosphere, and that this coupling drives global impacts.
Shows that El Niño breaks links in a global climate network, so its effects can reach well beyond the Pacific.
Finds tropical Atlantic sea surface temperature indices strongly persistent, so warm conditions tend to stay rather than spike and return.
Finds the 2023 global temperature jump was amplified by record low reflectivity, suggesting a forced push into a new level.
Shows climate subsystems can have multiple stable states and threshold tipping, so a persistent exceedance can signal a regime shift.
Shows current El Nino predictions lose skill after six months, a caveat for winter forecasts.
Gives a case where a seasonal model forecast La Nina while observations stayed normal, showing model bias can miss reality.
Record-low planetary albedo from fewer low clouds explains part of the recent surge beyond known drivers.
Shows record low cloud cover cut Earth's reflectivity, adding heat beyond trend and likely contributing to current ocean warmth.
Shows that El Niño and La Niña surface temperature impacts are localized and vary between events, cautioning against a simple global flip.
Forecast that the 2023 El Niño would raise global temperature about 0.2 °C, making 2024 hottest, matching the one-year lag in air records.
Peru bank data show El Niño changed spending and had a measurable recovery time, evidence of delayed regional economic impacts.
Shows 2023 record heat was partly from low clouds, a caveat when attributing a year-after El Niño temperature jump.
Shows upper-ocean warming and stratification change ENSO strength, so a warmer ocean alters the system forecasts must read.
Finds Parana River streamflow in southeastern South America tracks El Nino, a regional measure of rain linked to soybean areas.
Research finds El Niño reduces early postharvest conflict in Southern Africa croplands, showing impacts are not only crop losses.
Explains why recent warming was underestimated: a record-low planetary albedo from fewer low clouds added about 0.2°C that models missed.
Finds El Niño and La Niña shifts change postharvest conflict in Sahel crop areas, supporting a climate to harvest link in West Africa.
Independent 2026 forecast predicted neutral or weak El Niño, also below observed +1.80, so underprediction was widespread.
Explains how Niño 3.4 SST anomalies are estimated, so the observed ONI +1.80 depends on the anomaly method.
Shows Sahel heavy summer rainfall is linked to ENSO, with El Niño tending to suppress moisture and instability.
Measures ENSO effects on harvest-time conflict in Sahel croplands, noting early postharvest reductions.
Measures Iran's seasonal precipitation response to ENSO, PDO and NAO. It finds the Southern Oscillation Index has the strongest effect mainly in winter.
Adds background on early winter El Nino to North Atlantic Oscillation links and notes models find them hard to capture.
El Nino impacts differ for central versus eastern Pacific warming, so regional wet and dry patterns can shift.
It measures El Niño effects on winter temperatures in northern Eurasia, informing how mild European Russia winters really get.
It examines how predictable spring and summer climate anomalies in northern Eurasia are during El Niño, covering the spring signal.
It finds Paraná river streamflow rises with stronger solar activity and El Niño, backing flood risk in the Paraná basin.
Uses card transaction data to show how consumer spending and merchant activity changed in Peru after the 2017 El Niño floods.
Finds eastern Pacific El Niño events coincide with anomalous rainfall over larger areas than central Pacific events.
Measures how El Niño type changes where seasonal rainfall is very low or high, relevant to the Pacific dry and wet split.
It measures where El Niño and La Niña cause warming or cooling, showing these effects are concentrated in localized areas.
It explains that El Niño and La Niña are phases of a coupled ocean atmosphere cycle with global weather impacts.
Explains that strong El Niño timing is intrinsically unpredictable because the system shifts between oscillatory and chaotic states.
Uses climate networks to show El Niño breaks temperature correlation links globally, evidencing its wide weather reach.
Peruvian bank card data show El Niño rains altered buying patterns, grounding the local economic impact.
Separates central and eastern Pacific El Niño types, whose warming locations change which regions get wet or dry.
Shows how to estimate sea surface temperature anomalies in the Niño 3.4 region, the main measure the statement defines.
Uses temperature anomalies across the Niño 3.4 region to forecast El Niño onset and magnitude, supporting the region's central role.
Forecasts a 2023 El Niño magnitude at 1.49 degrees Celsius, near the strong threshold of 1.5 degrees.
Shows eastern Pacific El Nino events are a distinct type and can be forecast early, backing the dashboard's focus on the eastern band.
Explores how to estimate the climate baselines used to compute Niño 3.4 anomalies, which are the building blocks of the ONI.
Uses an east-west sea surface temperature difference to indicate whether an El Niño will be Eastern or Central Pacific type.
Shows an analogue method using past observations to forecast extremes without a climate model, though its focus is long term.
Uses the 1878 to 2013 SOI record as an ENSO descriptor and shows it holds nonlinear predictability years ahead.
Shows how climate trends bias simple normals and describes a filter to estimate anomalies after removing that trend.
Separates a small underlying warming trend from year to year variability when explaining the 1998 temperature record.
Explains how climate normals and anomalies are estimated, using Niño 3.4 sea surface temperatures as a test case.
Shows pure deep learning lacks data for extreme events, so it adds simulated data and physical laws to improve forecasts.
Finds statistical and physics models miss nonlinearity, so a data driven nonlinear model predicts better.
Tests a hybrid machine learning model and finds it struggles with nonlinear responses under warming outside its training data.
Shows how Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature normals and anomalies are estimated in real time, informing record and season comparisons.
Finds a cumulative Southern Oscillation index explains half of tropospheric temperature variation, supporting a delayed air response.
Describes the ocean to air energy exchange during El Nino events, the mechanism behind the delayed warming.
It uses a model where ocean heat builds and discharges, the idea behind warm water volume.
It shows that warming below the surface strengthens El Niño by increasing the layering of warm and cold water, so the ocean below the surface matters.
Models westerly wind bursts as wind stress noise that amplifies El Nino, with stronger events tied to more and stronger bursts.
Estimates climate normals and wind anomalies for Pacific trade winds, the basis for the sigma above normal threshold.
Finds El Niño mainly controls the seasonal timing of the Indian Ocean Dipole, supporting the link.
Shows El Niño wind patterns reach the Indian Ocean and set up the sea surface temperature pattern of the dipole.
Finds the dipole's effect on Indian rainfall is weak when El Niño is present, so the monsoon response is dominated by El Niño.
Observed shifts in extreme tropical rainfall between wet and dry regions with ENSO phases support the drought and flood link.
Peru's 2017 El Niño floods changed household spending, showing how flood impacts reach people through the economy.
Provides a coupled model where MJO wind forcing interacts with ENSO, useful for the timing pushes.
Models MJO eastward propagation coupled to ENSO, capturing wind interactions behind the timing pushes.
Near surface air temperature networks show El Niño warming or cooling is localized and varies by event, so fixed land boxes catch only some regions.
El Niño type, eastern or central Pacific, can flip a region between dry and wet conditions, so box responses vary by event.
Provides a mathematical theory of Walker circulation shifts between normal and El Nino states, supporting the collapse interpretation.
Finds strong coupling of the El Nino region to a second temperature mode in normal or La Nina phases, linked to a strong Walker circulation.
Uses a recharge oscillator model to show strong El Nino events can switch unpredictably, so past events may not guide peak strength.
Finds forecast models miss observed ENSO nonlinearity, causing skill limits; a nonlinear model improves predictions.
Strong El Niño events can switch irregularly between oscillatory and chaotic states, limiting predictability even with good models.
Hybrid model corrects climate model biases and captures warm versus cold asymmetry, improving strong event forecasts.
Shows how central Pacific sea surface temperatures drive deep convection and affect the Walker and Hadley circulations.
Explains how the Walker circulation changes state and drives El Niño oscillations.
Uses near-surface air temperature networks to show El Niño warming and cooling is localized, not uniform globally.
Compares precipitation extremes during EP and CP events and finds EP impacts cover larger areas, supporting a harsher eastern type.
Notes CP El Niño events are typically weaker than EP events, linking the eastern type to stronger anomalies.
Shows EP and CP events have different regional impacts, with early type forecasts from Pacific SST differences.
Model produces separate EP and CP modes shaped by decadal Walker circulation shifts, offering a mechanism for the two flavors.
Shows low-cloud cover drives planetary albedo changes, supporting cloud share as an albedo proxy.
Shows a network method that forecasts the strength and timing of El Niño using Niño 3.4 temperature anomalies about one year ahead.
Finds that strong El Niño events can switch unpredictably, so a current Niño 3.4 anomaly does not guarantee future strength.
Shows how climate normals and anomalies are estimated and questions the standard 30 year baseline used for Niño indices.
Explains that strong El Niño events, which appear as large Niño 1+2 anomalies, can be intrinsically unpredictable.
Deep learning forecasts global monthly sea surface temperature anomalies up to 24 months with low error.
Finds that global sea surface warming happened in sharp steps, not smoothly, over the twentieth century.
Shows natural swings such as El Nino drive year to year global temperature changes, so a single warm or cool year is not the whole story.
Explains shifts in El Niño variance come from changing likelihoods of event types, a caveat for long Niño 3.4 records.
Shows strong El Niño onset can be intrinsically unpredictable, so Niño 3.4 anomalies alone may not give long lead warning.
Trains a neural network on Pacific sea surface temperatures to predict the Niño 3.4 index months ahead.
Uses temperature links across the Niño 3.4 region to forecast El Niño onset and size about one year ahead.
Finds that ENSO linked modes explain significant sea surface temperature variance in Indian Ocean Dipole regions in HadISST data.
Shows an analog method for temperature extremes, the same family as the analogue day method behind this Niño 3.4 forecast.
Shows a data-driven global ocean model forecasts 3D ocean dynamics on seasonal to decadal timescales.
Explains the analog forecasting method for temperature extremes, used here as background though it targets air not ocean.
Uses an analog method to forecast air temperature extremes, showing this approach can predict temperature patterns.
Proposes a statistical method for Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomalies, avoiding biases in standard 30 year normals.
Explains the physical mechanism behind SOI variability as slow atmospheric Rossby waves, matching observed periods.
Explains how equatorial Pacific wind variability drives thermocline shifts and ENSO on interannual timescales.
Links North Equatorial Counter Current temperatures to deep convection near the date line, seen in outgoing longwave radiation changes.
Shows accumulated ENSO explains half of tropospheric temperature variation, a key caveat for this lower troposphere metric.
Describes an analogue method for forecasting temperature extremes; useful background for analogue based peak estimates.
Measures the 2023 global temperature surge and attributes part of it to record low planetary albedo.
